title: ACT Science: Reading Data, Not Memorising It
summary: The ACT Science section — graphs, experiments and competing viewpoints — and why it tests data skills, not science facts (plus its new optional status).

chunks.heading: It's a data-reading test
chunks.body: ACT Science gives you **graphs, tables and experiment descriptions** and asks you to **interpret them** — trends, relationships, what an experiment showed. It requires **very little memorised science**; the skill is **reading data accurately and fast**.
chunks.realExample: A question might ask 'as temperature rises, what happens to the reaction rate?' — you read the trend off the graph, not recall chemistry. Get the axes and units right and the answer is there.
chunks.memoryHook: It tests reading data, not knowing science. Read the graph, not your memory.

chunks.heading: Three question formats
chunks.body: The section has three types: **Data Representation** (read graphs/tables), **Research Summaries** (interpret described experiments and their design), and **Conflicting Viewpoints** (compare two or more scientists' competing hypotheses). Each rewards careful reading of what's presented.
chunks.realExample: In Conflicting Viewpoints, keep each scientist's claim straight — a question may ask which viewpoint a new finding supports, and the trap is mixing up whose theory is whose.
chunks.memoryHook: Data, Experiments, Viewpoints. Keep each scientist's claim separate in Viewpoints.

chunks.heading: Read axes, units and labels first
chunks.body: Most mistakes come from **misreading the figure** — the axis, the units, or which line is which. Spend a couple of seconds **orienting to each graph** before answering; a single misread can sink several questions on the same figure.
chunks.realExample: If a y-axis is in 'thousands', an answer of '5' means 5,000 — reading the units once correctly protects the whole set of questions on that graph.
chunks.memoryHook: Orient to the figure first: axes, units, which line. One misread sinks the set.

chunks.heading: Now optional — but check your date
chunks.body: Under the **enhanced ACT, Science is becoming an optional section reported separately** (with a STEM score), rolling out through 2025–2026. Whether you need it depends on your **test date and target colleges** — many STEM programmes still value a Science score, so confirm before skipping it.
chunks.realExample: If you're applying to engineering or science programmes, a strong Science score can help even where it's optional — check each college's stance rather than assuming you can skip it.
chunks.memoryHook: Science is going optional (phased). STEM applicants: confirm before you skip it.

recall.q: What does the ACT Science section actually test?
recall.a: Your ability to read and interpret data — graphs, tables and experiments — with very little memorised science.

recall.q: What are the three ACT Science question formats?
recall.a: Data Representation, Research Summaries, and Conflicting Viewpoints.

recall.q: What's the key skill in Conflicting Viewpoints?
recall.a: Keeping each scientist's competing hypothesis straight so you can compare them accurately.

recall.q: What causes most ACT Science mistakes?
recall.a: Misreading the figure — the axes, units or which line is which — so orient to each graph first.

recall.q: What is the new status of the ACT Science section?
recall.a: It's becoming optional and reported separately (with a STEM score), phased through 2025–2026 — so confirm your test date and college requirements.
